```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
comment = NA, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 8, cache = FALSE)
```

_theft_ is an R package that gives a single, consistent interface for extracting time-series features.
It provides access to $\approx 6000$ features from existing R and Python packages, and lets you add your own features.
It takes a [tsibble](https://tsibble.tidyverts.org) (a tidy temporal data frame) and returns a tidy table of feature values, ready for analysis with its companion package [_theftdlc_](https://github.com/hendersontrent/theftdlc).

📖 **Full documentation:** [hendersontrent.github.io/theft](https://hendersontrent.github.io/theft/), including the vignette and function reference.
📄 **Paper:** ["Feature-Based Time-Series Analysis in R using the Theft Ecosystem"](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2025-023/) explains the motivation and theory behind _theft_ and walks through its functionality on the [Bonn EEG dataset](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11736210/), a well-studied neuroscience dataset.

## Installation

Install the stable version from CRAN:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("theft")
```

Or install the development version from GitHub:

```{r eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("hendersontrent/theft")
```

The R-based feature sets (`catch22`, `feasts`, `tsfeatures`) work straight away.
The Python-based sets (`kats`, `tsfresh`, `tsfel`, `hctsa`) need a Python installation, preferably Python 3.10 or newer.
_theft_ can create a virtual environment for you with the libraries it needs:

```{r eval = FALSE}
library(theft)

# Creates a virtual environment named "theft-package" with Kats, tsfresh and TSFEL.
# Set hctsa = TRUE to also install pyhctsa (large).
install_python_pkgs(venv = "theft-package", python = "/usr/local/bin/python3.10")

# Tell R to use that environment (once per R session)
init_theft("theft-package")
```

Each library also has its own installer (e.g., `install_tsfresh()`, `install_pyhctsa()`), with a matching `init_theft_*()` function.
See `?install_python_pkgs` and the vignette for details.

## Feature sets

Pass any of these names (or several at once) to the `feature_set` argument of `calculate_features()`.

| `feature_set` | Language | Source package | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"catch22"` | R | [_catch22_](https://github.com/DynamicsAndNeuralSystems/catch22) via [_Rcatch22_](https://github.com/hendersontrent/Rcatch22), the native R implementation on CRAN | 22 features (24 with `catch24 = TRUE`) |
| `"feasts"` | R | [_feasts_](https://feasts.tidyverts.org) | |
| `"tsfeatures"` | R | [_tsfeatures_](https://github.com/robjhyndman/tsfeatures) | |
| `"kats"` | Python | [_Kats_](https://facebookresearch.github.io/Kats/) | Installed from [`hendersontrent/theft-kats`](https://github.com/hendersontrent/theft-kats) |
| `"tsfresh"` | Python | [_tsfresh_](https://tsfresh.readthedocs.io) | |
| `"tsfel"` | Python | [_TSFEL_](https://tsfel.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) | |
| `"hctsa"` | Python | [_pyhctsa_](https://github.com/DynamicsAndNeuralSystems/pyhctsa), the Python port of [_hctsa_](https://github.com/benfulcher/hctsa) (originally MATLAB) | Large feature set |

Four simple baseline sets are also available, for comparing against the more sophisticated sets (see [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17809) for the idea):

| `feature_set` | Contents |
|---|---|
| `"fft"` | 200 features: the squared magnitude and the angle of FFT coefficients 0 to 99 |
| `"quantiles"` | 101 quantiles |
| `"fftquantiles"` | The union of `"fft"` and `"quantiles"` |
| `"moments"` | The first four moments of the distribution: mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis |

You can also compute your own features by passing a named list of functions to the `features` argument (see the quick tour below).
For a comprehensive comparison of six of these feature sets across a range of domains (computation speed, within-set feature composition, and between-set feature correlations), see [An Empirical Evaluation of Time-Series Feature Sets](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9679937).

## The _theft_ ecosystem

The companion package [_theftdlc_](https://github.com/hendersontrent/theftdlc) ("_theft_ downloadable content", just like the [DLC](https://en.bandainamcoent.eu/elden-ring/elden-ring/shadow-of-the-erdtree) you get for video games) contains a suite of functions for analyzing, interpreting, and visualizing the features that _theft_ calculates.
Collectively, the two packages are the "_theft_ ecosystem".
From `v0.6.1`, _theft_ performs feature extraction only, and many functions that used to live in _theft_ are now in _theftdlc_ under other names.

<img src="man/figures/theft-packages.png" alt="Hex stickers of the theft and theftdlc packages for R" />

A high-level view of how the ecosystem is typically used:

<img src="man/figures/workflow-graphic_ecosystem-final.png" alt="Schematic of the theft ecosystem in R" />

Many more functions and options are available in the packages; explore the vignettes and help files for more.

## Quick tour

_theft_ and _theftdlc_ combine into an efficient workflow consistent with the broader [tidyverts](https://tidyverts.org) collection of packages for tidy time-series analysis.
The code below calculates features for a tsibble of simulated time series (Gaussian noise, AR(1), ARMA(1,1), MA(1), noisy sinusoid, and a random walk; `simData` comes with _theft_).
We use the _catch22_ feature set and a custom set of the mean and standard deviation, then feed the features straight into `project()` from _theftdlc_, which projects the 24-dimensional feature space into two dimensions using principal components analysis:

```{r pca-example, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
library(dplyr)
library(theft)
library(theftdlc)

calculate_features(data = theft::simData, 
                   feature_set = "catch22",
                   features = list("mean" = mean, "sd" = sd)) %>%
  project(norm_method = "RobustSigmoid",
          unit_int = TRUE,
          low_dim_method = "PCA") %>%
  plot()
```

Here `calculate_features()` comes from _theft_, while `project()` and the `plot()` method come from _theftdlc_.

In the same way, we can compare the time-series classification performance of _catch22_ against our custom set of the first two moments:

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
calculate_features(data = theft::simData, 
                   feature_set = "catch22",
                   features = list("mean" = mean, "sd" = sd)) %>%
  classify(by_set = TRUE,
           n_resamples = 10,
           use_null = TRUE) %>%
  compare_features(by_set = TRUE,
                   hypothesis = "pairwise") %>%
  head()
```

`classify()` and `compare_features()` come from _theftdlc_.

We can also see how each set performs relative to an empirical null distribution (i.e., how much better each set does than expected by chance):

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
calculate_features(data = theft::simData, 
                   feature_set = "catch22",
                   features = list("mean" = mean, "sd" = sd)) %>%
  classify(by_set = TRUE,
           n_resamples = 10,
           use_null = TRUE) %>%
  compare_features(by_set = TRUE,
                   hypothesis = "null") %>%
  head()
```

See the [vignette](https://hendersontrent.github.io/theft/articles/theft.html) for more information and the full functionality of both packages.
